_comment: Extinct taxa. A fossil is a tip that stops short of the present, so it needs
three ages, not one:
splitAge   when its lineage diverged from its sister. Constrains the topology.
firstAppearance  oldest occurrence in the rock record.
lastAppearance   youngest occurrence. The tip is drawn terminating here.
The gap between splitAge and firstAppearance is the ghost lineage, and the app
draws it as a thin line so students can see how much of a branch is inference
rather than fossils.
Attachment. Exactly one of:
attachStemOf      a backbone node id from backbone.json. The fossil becomes
sister to that node at splitAge. Several fossils on the same
stem nest automatically: the builder sorts by splitAge
descending, so the oldest divergence ends up outermost.
attachStemOfMRCA  a list of living species names. The fossil becomes sister to
their most recent common ancestor. This is how an extinct
lineage gets placed inside a grafted clade tree.
grades  a list of grade ids from grades.json. Grades are paraphyletic by
construction and may nest, so a taxon can belong to more than one.
Ages are approximate, rounded, and mostly stage-level. They are for teaching,
not for calibration. Where placement is genuinely contested the note says so and
an entry in alternatives.json usually offers the competing arrangement.

fossils.label: Conodonta
fossils.note: Eel-like animals known mostly from phosphatic feeding elements. Usually placed as stem vertebrates or stem gnathostomes; the soft-bodied specimens from the Granton Shrimp Bed settled that they are chordates but not much more.

fossils.label: Myllokunmingia
fossils.note: Chengjiang, Cambrian Stage 3. Among the oldest animals with a recognisable vertebrate body plan. Haikouichthys is very likely the same thing.

fossils.label: Pteraspidomorphi
fossils.note: Includes Arandaspida, Astraspida and Heterostraci. Paired nostrils absent; the head shield is built from dentine-bearing plates.

fossils.label: Thelodonti
fossils.note: Scale-covered rather than plate-armoured, and probably paraphyletic themselves. Shown here as one lineage for legibility.

fossils.label: Galeaspida
fossils.note: Almost entirely Chinese and Vietnamese. Shuyu braincase material has been central to reconstructing the jawless-to-jawed transition.

fossils.label: Pituriaspida
fossils.note: Two species, both Devonian, both from Queensland. Included to show how thin some of these branches really are.

fossils.label: Osteostraci
fossils.note: The closest jawless relatives of jawed vertebrates. Paired pectoral fins and a perichondrally ossified endoskeleton both appear here, before jaws do.

fossils.label: Antiarchi
fossils.note: Jointed, arthropod-like pectoral appendages. Bothriolepis is one of the most abundant Devonian vertebrate genera anywhere.

fossils.label: Ptyctodontida
fossils.note: Tooth plates and claspers. Long mistaken for early holocephalans on those grounds.

fossils.label: Arthrodira
fossils.note: The largest placoderm radiation. Dunkleosteus terrelli reached six metres and sheared with bone blades rather than teeth.

fossils.label: Entelognathus
fossils.note: A placoderm with maxilla, premaxilla and dentary, the marginal jaw bones previously thought diagnostic of bony fishes. This single specimen is most of the reason placoderms are now read as a grade rather than a clade.

fossils.label: Acanthodiformes
fossils.note: Acanthodes bronni braincase material is what moved acanthodians from stem osteichthyans to stem chondrichthyans.

fossils.label: Cladoselache
fossils.note: Cleveland Shale. Preserved with fin outlines and gut contents, which is why it appears in every textbook despite being one genus.

fossils.label: Xenacanthiformes
fossils.note: Freshwater, with a distinctive occipital spine.

fossils.label: Hybodontiformes
fossils.note: The dominant Mesozoic sharks. They persist right to the K-Pg and then do not.

fossils.label: Palaeonisciformes
fossils.note: A wastebasket grade of early ray-finned fishes, not a clade. Retained here precisely because grades of this kind are what the scaffold is meant to handle.

fossils.label: Osteolepiformes
fossils.note: Eusthenopteron foordi has humerus, radius and ulna in a fin. Vertebrate anatomy courses have been built on this one animal for a century.

fossils.label: Tiktaalik
fossils.note: A mobile neck, a flat head and a weight-bearing forefin. Found by predicting the rock: Late Devonian, non-marine, and exposed. Ellesmere Island, 2004.

fossils.label: Elpistostege
fossils.note: The 2020 complete specimen shows phalanges inside the fin, before any animal had left the water.

fossils.label: Acanthostega
fossils.note: Eight digits per hand, internal gills, and a limb that could not have carried it on land. Limbs evolved in water and were later co-opted, not built for walking.

fossils.label: Temnospondyli
fossils.note: Placed on the lissamphibian stem under the temnospondyl hypothesis, which is the majority position. Koolasuchus from the Australian Early Cretaceous is the youngest. The lissamphibian-origins toggle moves this branch.

fossils.label: Lepospondyli
fossils.note: Under the competing lepospondyl hypothesis, lissamphibians nest inside this group instead. Shown here as a stem lineage; see the lissamphibian-origins toggle.

fossils.label: Diadectomorpha
fossils.note: The closest relatives of amniotes, and among the first terrestrial vertebrate herbivores.

fossils.label: Sphenacodontidae
fossils.note: Dimetrodon is a closer relative of you than of any dinosaur, and predates all of them. Worth saying out loud in a lecture.

fossils.label: Anomodontia
fossils.note: Dicynodonts. Lystrosaurus dominates Early Triassic assemblages after the end-Permian extinction to a degree nothing else matches.

fossils.label: Tritylodontidae
fossils.note: Herbivorous cynodonts that outlast the origin of mammals by a wide margin.

fossils.label: Morganucodonta
fossils.note: Dentary-squamosal jaw joint alongside the old quadrate-articular one. The transition is visible in a single skull.

fossils.label: Multituberculata
fossils.note: The longest-lived mammalian order, roughly 130 million years, and entirely extinct. Their position relative to the mammalian crown is not settled.

fossils.label: Pappochelys
fossils.note: Broadened ribs and gastralia, no shell. The turtle shell assembles in stages and this is an early one.

fossils.label: Odontochelys
fossils.note: Plastron present, carapace absent, teeth still in the jaws. Bottom half first.

fossils.label: Proganochelys
fossils.note: A complete shell, but the neck cannot retract.

fossils.label: Meiolaniidae
fossils.note: Horned stem turtles that survived on Lord Howe, New Caledonia and Vanuatu until roughly 3,000 years ago, which is to say until people arrived. A stem lineage can outlast most of the crown.

fossils.label: Phytosauria
fossils.note: Crocodile-shaped, crocodile-sized, not crocodiles. The nostrils sit back near the eyes rather than at the snout tip.

fossils.label: Thalattosuchia
fossils.note: Fully marine crocodylomorphs with paddle limbs and a tail fluke.

fossils.label: Notosuchia
fossils.note: Terrestrial, often herbivorous, mostly Gondwanan. Some had mammal-like occlusion.

fossils.label: Deinosuchus
fossils.note: Long read as an alligatoroid. Walter et al. 2025 recover it outside crown Crocodylia, which also implies saltwater tolerance was ancestral and lost later in alligatorids.

fossils.label: Pterosauria
fossils.note: Sister to dinosaurs, not inside them. Powered flight in vertebrates evolved at least three separate times: here, in birds, and in bats.

fossils.label: Oviraptorosauria
fossils.note: Brooding postures preserved on nests. The behaviour is older than the crown group.

fossils.label: Archaeopteryx
fossils.note: Twelve or so specimens, all from the Solnhofen limestone, all within about half a million years. The most consequential single locality in vertebrate palaeontology.

fossils.label: Confuciusornithidae
fossils.note: The first toothless beak in the bird lineage.

fossils.label: Enantiornithes
fossils.note: The dominant land birds of the Cretaceous, and they do not cross the K-Pg boundary. Every living bird descends from the other branch.

fossils.label: Hesperornithiformes
fossils.note: Flightless, foot-propelled marine divers with teeth.

fossils.label: Ichthyornithiformes
fossils.note: The closest well-known relative of crown birds. Modern wing, modern brain shape, and a mouth full of teeth.

fossils.label: Mosasauria
fossils.note: Placed here as sister to Anguimorpha, which is the common molecular-scaffold result. A competing morphological position puts mosasaurs with snakes. Either way they sit inside Squamata, which is the point: a famous extinct radiation nested among living lizards.

fossils.label: Ichthyosauria
fossils.note: Placement is genuinely unresolved. Shown on the lepidosaur stem as a diapsid of uncertain position; treat this branch as a placeholder rather than a result.

fossils.label: Sauropterygia
fossils.note: Plesiosaurs, pliosaurs and placodonts. Often recovered near or within Archelosauria, but with low support. Another placeholder branch.

fossils.label: Dinornithiformes
fossils.note: Nine species, flightless, New Zealand, gone within about 150 years of Polynesian settlement. Sister to tinamous, which means flight was lost independently several times among palaeognaths.

fossils.label: Aepyornithidae
fossils.note: Madagascan, up to half a tonne, and the closest living relatives are the kiwi of New Zealand. Vicariance does not explain that distribution; independent loss of flight after dispersal does.

fossils.label: Raphus cucullatus
fossils.note: A large flightless pigeon from Mauritius, last credibly recorded around 1662. Nearest living relative is the Nicobar pigeon.

fossils.label: Pinguinus impennis
fossils.note: Last confirmed pair killed on Eldey, Iceland, in June 1844.

fossils.label: Hydrodamalis gigas
fossils.note: Described in 1741, extinct by about 1768. Twenty-seven years from first description to last animal.

fossils.label: Mammuthus primigenius
fossils.note: Nested with Asian rather than African elephants. The Wrangel Island population persists to roughly 4,000 years ago, well into the Bronze Age.

fossils.label: Smilodon fatalis
fossils.note: Machairodontinae, sister to all living cats rather than inside them.
